label: Trading places — the seesaw
vo: It's not a coincidence that two things often trade places in public opinion and in reality.

label: The scientists triumphant — hers
vo: If science had a battle cry, it would be stop all this nonsense,

label: The ever formidable woo — hers
vo: folkism, superstition, and the ever formidable woo. We've put up with nonsense for far too long.

label: The empty magician's hat
vo: Now it's time to stop all this hocus pocus and face the facts. Matter is matter and that's all we've got.

label: She is trying to fit in — hers
vo: And I, as a young woman in a male world wanting so badly to be respected, not to be one of those who believed in silly things like magic and God, accepted this ill-gotten premonition into every pore till it oozed out.

label: Candles for a lightbulb
vo: We had magic because we were scared. We couldn't explain everything. Now we have science so we don't need magic anymore. And anyone who thinks we do is stupid and wrong.

label: The beautiful method — glass sieves
vo: But here's where things get tricky because science doesn't have a battle cry because it's not really an it, instead it's a method, a way of conducting experiments that eliminates as many variables as possible.

label: One thing known for sure
vo: In theory, it's rather beautiful. The idea that we could, the idea that we, the idea that we could know something, even one thing for sure, gets more and more magnificent the longer you think about it.

label: A cathedral of knowledge
vo: And the harder you realize it is to know anything, anything at all. And then that all this knowledge could build up on itself and form these coherent systems.

label: The balcony proclamation
vo: We did a study, say scientists in white coats in labs somewhere, in some lab somewhere, and now we know this thing.

label: MORE WATER! RIGHT NOW! — hers
vo: Sometimes it's just common sense. It turns out drinking more water is actually really good for you and for all these various reasons. So everyone should do it a lot.

label: A staircase into the clouds
vo: But we know it's just one step in a long chain of steps and that we're getting closer to knowing everything.

label: Findings shoved in her face — hers
vo: In fact, they could say almost anything. And I, like most people, would believe it,

label: Dino nuggets from the sky — hers
vo: delivering these nuggets of truth and wisdom

label: Dino nuggets, everyone amazed — hers
vo: that we no longer have to worry about, like manna from the sky.

label: Dinner with the PhD student
vo: The first time I really questioned this system was when I dated a PhD student at UCLA.

label: Scientists hiding in a corner — hers
vo: And he mentioned casually in passing that all their numbers were wrong. Evidently, his advisor had been fudging the numbers for years.

label: Seven years — a fork in the road
vo: Now, seven years into his PhD, he was faced with a moral conundrum. I'll spare you the conclusion or any of the names involved.

label: Reading The Blank Slate at night
vo: In a rather dark hour, I read almost the entirety of Steven Pinker's The Blank Slate, a devout atheist. I was almost giggling to myself when I read the chapter on the various causes of our personality as children.

label: The last puzzle piece glows
vo: He goes into great detail, explaining the common non-influences that have proven to have no effect—parents, images, and the media—but makes it clear that there is 10% of inexplicables that cannot be explained in any one way.

label: Identical twins, different shadows
vo: Even in identical twins, they differ from birth in this mysterious 10th percentage.

label: The soul rising from the book
vo: Given my aforementioned desperate fear of even suggesting something supernatural, I was almost embarrassed on his account for how strongly this suggested the existence of a soul. And yet, somehow, he confidently finished the chapter without giving any additional explanation for this now most mysterious 10% of ambiguity.

label: Every door opens on stars
vo: Is it just me, or does every new bit of science we uncover prove, more and more, the existence of magic and of God?

label: The double slit and the eye
vo: I came across a YouTube short the other day saying they did an experiment—a second version of the slit experiment—in which they decided whether to observe after the fact, and particles behaved as waves or particles depending on whether they decided to observe it after the

label: Time runs backwards
vo: Meaning, while I'm not entirely sure what it means, that time travel is possible?

label: Rockefeller ransacks the herb garden
vo: After Rockefeller casually ransacked our age-old herbalism tradition in favor of newer and more modern and better ones, scientists have been discovering the health benefits of things like turmeric and St. John's wort.

label: The golden thread pulled from the tapestry
vo: What I find especially worth noting is that turmeric works best as a whole plant, when taken with animal fat and pepper. However, scientists, in their infinite pursuit of specificity, have disentangled the active compound curcumin from the plant, making it less effective.

label: The willow gives its bark
vo: Similarly, white willow bark, from which is derived salicylic acid, the active compound in aspirin, manages to steer clear of things like stomach ulcers, the side effects of aspirin, when taken as a whole plant.

label: The wildflower lifts her out
vo: And St. John's wort, a naturally occurring SSRI, is much easier to get off of than, say, Prozac.

label: The brother and the magnifying glass
vo: My brother, a hard-minded materialist, agrees that plants might have amazing healing potential, but he just wishes scientists would have more time to study them. That would be nice, wouldn't it? To be able to name all the chemicals before we put them in our body?

label: The tangled web of compounds
vo: The problem, I think, is the sheer number of compounds, not to mention their interactions.
